intro: Every conversation starts the same way: someone says hello. In Spanish, that first moment carries a lot. The greeting changes with the time of day, from buenos días (good morning) to buenas noches (good evening). The word for you changes with the person, from tú for a friend to usted for a teacher. A handshake, a hug or a cheek kiss may come with it.

This unit follows students meeting new people in Chicago, from Pilsen to Humboldt Park. You will greet and say goodbye, introduce a friend, and ask ¿Cómo te llamas? (What's your name?). You will spell names aloud with the 27 letters of the Spanish alphabet, and learn why many people carry two last names.

By the end, you will be able to meet someone new in Spanish, politely and correctly. You will ask where they are from with ¿De dónde eres?, name a nationality that matches the person, and write names with every accent mark in place. Those small marks matter: papá is dad, but papa is potato.
bigQuestion: How do the first words we say to someone show who we are and how much we respect them?

timeline.t: Antonio de Nebrija publishes the first grammar of the Castilian Spanish language
The first part of Don Quijote by Miguel de Cervantes is published
The Real Academia Española (RAE) is founded in Madrid
Mexico wins its independence from Spain
The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo moves a large part of Mexico's northern land to the United States
After the Spanish-American War, Puerto Rico becomes a U.S. territory
The Jones Act makes Puerto Ricans U.S. citizens
The Association of Academies of the Spanish Language is founded in Mexico
The academies' spelling guide sets the Spanish alphabet at 27 letters, without ch and ll

words.d: good morning — from waking up until about noon
good afternoon — from about noon until dark
good evening, good night — hello or goodbye after dark
see you later — a friendly goodbye
you (informal) — for friends, family and kids
you (formal) — for teachers, older adults and strangers
nice to meet you — said at a first meeting
let me introduce … to you (informal); formal: le presento a
How is it spelled? — ask it to spell a name correctly
the last name — many people have two: father's, then mother's
Where are you from? — answer Soy de…
the accent mark — changes stress or meaning: papá, papa

test.q: It is 7:30 a.m. Which greeting fits?
test.why: Buenos días is the morning greeting, and día is masculine.

test.q: Which word for you do you use with a new school principal?
test.why: Usted is the formal you, used to show respect.

test.q: You introduce your friend to your cousin. What do you say?
choices: Le presento a mi amiga Sara.
Te presento a mi amiga Sara.
test.why: With a cousin, use the informal te presento a.

test.q: Someone says "Mucho gusto." Which reply fits?
test.why: Igualmente means likewise, the usual reply to mucho gusto.

test.q: Which answer to ¿Cómo estás? is correct?
test.why: For how you feel, use estoy: Estoy bien.

test.q: Which letter does Spanish have that English lacks?
test.why: Ñ is the extra letter; ch and ll are digraphs, not letters.

test.q: How do you ask a new classmate's name?
test.why: ¿Cómo te llamas? is the informal way to ask a name.

test.q: Carmen López Reyes. Which last name traditionally comes from her father?
test.why: The first apellido traditionally comes from the father.

test.q: How do you politely greet Carmen López Reyes?
test.why: Use señora with the first apellido, López.
Origin uses ser plus de: Soy de Cuba.

test.q: Pablo is from Spain. What is his nationality?
test.why: The male form is español, in lowercase.

test.q: What does sí (with an accent) mean?
test.why: Sí means yes; si without the accent means if.

test.q: Which country is a Spanish-speaking country in Europe?
test.why: España is the only country in Europe with Spanish as its official language.

test.q: Which greeting custom does the unit describe?
choices: A light cheek kiss is common in many places, with customs that vary.
test.why: Cheek kisses are common in many places, but customs vary by country, family and person.

write.prompt: Escribe un párrafo: preséntate a una persona nueva. In Spanish, write 5 to 7 sentences. Greet the person for the time of day, say your name and spell it, say where you are from and your nationality, introduce a friend with te presento a or le presento a, and say goodbye.
tips: Choose tú or usted for the person and keep it the same the whole time.
Use soy de for where you are from, not estoy de.
Make your nationality match you, and write it in lowercase.
Check every accent mark and ñ, like in adiós, mañana and your own name.
Read it aloud as if you were really meeting the person.
